questions.question: What clinical features helped distinguish Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis from other causes of sepsis in this patient, and why is rapid identification of this organism important for management?
Which laboratory findings during the ICU course first suggested the development of a thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) rather than ongoing DIC, and how did they change the diagnostic approach?

Explain the pathophysiological mechanism by which complement‑mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome (CM‑HUS) can be triggered by an infection such as C. canimorsus, including the role of the alternative complement pathway.
Why was thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) considered unlikely in this patient, and what clinical score and laboratory value were most decisive?
What are the key histopathologic findings on renal biopsy that confirm TMA in the setting of CM‑HUS, and why were immune complex deposits ruled out?
Discuss the rationale for initiating plasma exchange (PEX) before starting eculizumab in this patient, including its potential benefits and limitations in CM‑HUS.
What infectious risks are associated with eculizumab therapy, and how were these risks mitigated in the management of this patient?

Describe how the alternative pathway activity assay (AH50) result influenced the interpretation of complement dysregulation in this patient, and why the result might have been affected by earlier treatments.
If this patient had shown pathogenic variants in complement factor H or factor I, how might that have changed her long‑term management plan?
What are the clinical and laboratory criteria for diagnosing meningococcal risk when starting a complement inhibitor, and how were these criteria applied before initiating eculizumab?
